newsitem.title: HONDURAS: Honduras frees former Haitian police chief.
newsitem.headline: Honduras frees former Haitian police chief.

text.p: Former Haitian police chief Col. Joseph Michel Francois walked out of prison Thursday, two days after the United States lost a final bid to have him extradited on drug charges.
"He has just left the Central Penitentiary after they handed him his letter of freedom," prison official Alan Reyes told Reuters.
Francois, 39, a leader in the 1991 coup against former Haitian President Jean-Bertrand Aristide, was a key member of the 1991-94 military government that stepped down under threat of a U.S. invasion.

The Honduran Supreme Court of Justice Tuesday rejected by a 5-4 vote one final U.S. appeal to extradite Francois to the United States, upholding lower court rulings that the U.S. case lacked evidence.
The United States accused Francois of organising cocaine shipments to U.S. soil while he held his former post as chief of the Port-au-Prince police.
The Francois case strained relations between the United States and Honduras, a small, poor Central American country.
U.S. officials stopped just short of accusing Honduras of harbouring an international criminal, while Honduran judges defended their decision as upholding the rule of law.

"The ruling was applied in this case with strict adherence to the law, the (extradition) treaty and our constitution," Miguel Rivera, president of the Supreme Court, told reporters on Thursday. "They (the Americans) should respect it."
Francois had been jailed since March 7 when he was arrested by Honduran authorities at the request of the Americans. He arrived in Honduras from the Dominican Republic in April 1996.
The United States said Wednesday it was "deeply disappointed" with the Supreme Court ruling and said it won't give up trying to bring Francois to justice.

U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said that "if Francois is allowed to enjoy impunity, it will be a signal that the Honduran government is ready to serve as a haven for drug criminals." Francois has said he plans to return to
the northern Honduran city of San Pedro Sula, where he owns a furniture shop.
